title: How to Write Matthew from Revelation: The Generative Grammar of the First Gospel (EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: HOW TO WRITE MATTHEW FROM REVELATION. The paper asks what a writer holding the Apocalypse of John, whole, would have to do to get a Gospel, and answers by doing it. The received account is stated first and in full: Matthew from Mark, a sayings source and material of its own; nothing passing from Revelation to Matthew; where the two agree, a common stock. The paper does not begin by disputing that. It takes Revelation as a source and works with it. Each section takes places of Revelation, states an operation, performs it, and sets the result beside Matthew's Greek: give the speaker a past; give the life a beginning, a land, a teaching, an economy and adversaries; turn the name into a story; make the end of the world a parable; open the tomb. The procedure is then stated as nine steps and twenty-one rules (T_Μ v0.4): the source held whole with the relation as its unit; three parameters (a past, a named land, and the layers Revelation was itself made from, scripture and Philo, standing open at each place); seven moves; five forms; five checks. Its evidence is a ledger of 86 relations, each checked for shared lemmas in a tagged text, reaching 178 of Matthew's 1,067 verses. One passage, the labourers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16), was produced by blind readers given Revelation 22:13 and 3:21 and the rule, under a key committed by hash, and by neither verse alone. Philo is admitted only through a place Revelation holds; six of seven sealed predictions on that parameter held, and the free test of Philo against Matthew was emptied by its control. A sealed prediction that the plagues give the miracles failed and is reported, with what the procedure does not reach: most of what Matthew shares with Mark, and Matthew 15 entire. The paper states that every pairing can be read in the other direction and that the procedure does not decide which book was written first; that argument is the programme's (Revelation First, #202, #1735, #1755). Section I.6 sets the paper beside Bultmann, Vos and Bauckham, each at the grain at which it could be read. With two figures, an appendix printing what the readers produced, and a packet for machine readers. 321 Greek quotations verified by machine against the seated texts (221 at v1.0). Part of the Revelation First programme; the relations are compressed with the programme's other mappings in the relations hologram, deposited after this record. Version 1.1 (27 November 2026, in place) rehearses the argument the demonstration sits inside (the literary-genetic argument; how Revelation was kept from candidacy as a source; why the reach matters), adds a section showing that Matthew handles Revelation as it handles the scripture it does not name, operation by operation beside the Septuagint, and brings the ledger to 158 relations reaching 305 of Matthew's 1,067 verses (86 and 178 at v1.0). It reports that no order of Revelation is kept in Matthew except one walk through the infancy, and that a count meant to decide direction did not. Version 2.1 (27 November 2026, in place) lays three bodies of extant text beside Revelation and reads them against Matthew the same way: the letters, Josephus, and the Gospel of Thomas as a second book read against the same source. It keeps two measures apart. The derivation is the ledger, unchanged at 158 relations and 305 verses (28.6 per cent), each relation with its move. The map is named pairs whose words stand in both texts, sealed as lists before checking, which with the ledger reach 659 to 693 of Matthew's 1,067 verses (61.8 to 64.9 per cent) at a looser standard, from one reader, with no test of direction. The sources posited behind the Gospels are set beside extant candidates, function by function, with a note of which have a count behind them and which have none. No hypothetical source is supposed for the remainder, which is held open as unexplained. No received date and no order of the Gospels is taken as a premise.

substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). The programme, the question, the method's direction and every ruling are Lee Sharks's, given in session on 26 and 27 November 2026 and recorded with their times in the working notebook (The Unfolding Map). The prose was drafted in session by Claude (TACHYON; Anthropic) at the author's word and under the author's rulings; the counts, the ledger checks and the verification of the 221 quotations were run in session by script; the blind runs were made by Claude models (Fable, Opus, Sonnet) as readers given a pack and nothing else; reviews by ChatGPT (LABOR) and Gemini were pasted by the author, checked item by item and incorporated. For v2.1 the new sections were drafted the same way from the working notebook (The Unfolding Map v0.81), the lists of pairs were made from memory by Claude as reader and checked by script against the seated texts, and a review of the v2.0 draft pasted by the author was checked item by item, found right on seven repairs including one miscount, and incorporated. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is credited because the paper is built from its deposits, seats and protocols.
methodology: A procedure is stated and run. Relations in Revelation and Matthew are paired by quotation, each pair checked for shared lemmas in a tagged Greek text (Tischendorf) and quoted from Nestle 1904 as seated; the Septuagint from Swete and Philo from Cohn–Wendland as seated. Every quotation was verified by script as a contiguous token sequence in its seat. Predictions were written to a sealed file with the clock time before each count or search; the tally of held and failed is given. One rule was given to blind readers with a place of Revelation, with cuts and controls, and scored from a key whose SHA-256 is printed in the paper; the key is withheld while runs are owed. Reach is counted over Matthew's 1,067 verses and by a machine proxy for material shared with Mark, shared with Luke, and Matthew's own. Works not obtainable without a paywall are declared and reported at the grain at which they were read. At v2.1: pairs of a passage of Matthew and a passage of a letter, of Josephus (Niese, as seated) or of the Septuagint were named by a reader, sealed as a list with predictions before any check, and checked for shared lemmas or word families by a stated rule; the rule's acceptance of exchanged pairings was measured (19 per cent as sealed, 1 per cent for a stricter rule) and both totals are given. Word families and oppositions are from MACULA Greek's tagging of the Nestle 1904 text and were tested against shuffled pairings. Controls are Greek prose outside the hypothesized system (Epictetus, Diodorus, Strabo, Maximus of Tyre); Josephus and Acts are not used as controls.
falsification_conditions: A quotation not found in its seat, or a ledger row whose shared lemmas are absent from the tagged text, fails that row. The inverse rule (parable to saying), written down, sealed and run with cuts, and accounting for where the sayings stand in Revelation's letters, would stand the demonstration of sections I and VII beside an equal. The same procedure run from another source of like length and reaching as much of Matthew would empty the reach. A control showing that the places in Philo cluster by treatise no more than chance would withdraw what the paper says of that clustering. The paper does not claim the order of composition, so no dating result falsifies it; a dating result bears on the programme (#1735). At v2.1: a second reader's lists, made blind to these, that do not reproduce the division of labour among Revelation, the letters and Josephus, or the shared verses of Revelation between Thomas and the Matthew ledger, would withdraw those two findings as the first reader's habit. A named pair whose words are absent from the seated texts fails that pair. An extant text outside the system reaching as much of Matthew by the same rule would empty the map.

wiki_article:
**How to Write Matthew from Revelation: The Generative Grammar of the First Gospel** (EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01) is a paper by Lee Sharks, published in *Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology* and deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 27 November 2026, with the archive and Claude (TACHYON; Anthropic) credited as contributors. It belongs to the Revelation First programme (#202), which holds that the Apocalypse of John is the generative source of the rest of the New Testament, and it is the programme's first worked case for a Gospel.

The paper states the received account first: Matthew made from Mark, a sayings source and its own material, with nothing passing from Revelation to Matthew. It then asks what a writer holding Revelation whole would have to do to obtain a Gospel, and answers by performing the operations. Each section takes places of Revelation, names an operation and sets the result beside Matthew's Greek: the speaker is given a past, the life a beginning, a land, a teaching, an economy and adversaries; the title "the first and the last" becomes the story of the labourers in the vineyard; the end of the world becomes a parable; the tomb is opened.

The procedure is given as nine steps and twenty-one rules, called T_Μ at version 0.4. Its evidence is a ledger of 86 relations, each checked for shared lemmas in a tagged Greek text, reaching 178 of Matthew's 1,067 verses. One passage, Matthew 20:1–16, was produced by blind readers given Revelation 22:13 and 3:21 and the rule, and by neither verse alone, under a scoring key committed by its SHA-256. A third parameter opens the layers Revelation was itself made from, scripture and Philo of Alexandria, at places Revelation holds; the places in Philo are those of In the Midst of the Seven (#1758). Six of seven sealed predictions on that parameter held. A free test of Philo against Matthew was emptied by its control, and a sealed prediction that the plagues yield the miracles failed; both are reported.

The paper says what it does not show. Every pairing can be read in the other direction, and the procedure does not decide which book was written first; that argument is made in Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles (#1735) and mapped in the framework hologram (#1755). Most of what Matthew shares with Mark is not reached, and Matthew 15 has no row. Section I.6 places the paper beside Bultmann, Vos and Bauckham, each reported at the grain at which it could be read without a paywall. The method follows the archive's earlier Sappho–Philo transforms (#1486, #1494). The paper carries two figures, an appendix printing the readers' output, and a packet for machine readers. Version 1.1, reissued in place on 27 November 2026, sets the demonstration inside the argument of the Revelation First programme and keeps apart what the paper shows, what the programme holds on grounds argued in other records, and what the programme claims it will show. Its new section on scripture sets five operations Matthew performs on the Septuagint at undisputed places (a phrase kept, a saying staged as an event, a scene told again with another bearer, two scriptures in one line, scripture turned in the open) beside the same operations performed on Revelation. The ledger stands at 158 relations reaching 305 of Matthew's 1,067 verses. The paper reports that Matthew draws on Revelation in no order, as it draws on Isaiah and the Psalms, with one exception in the infancy narrative, and that the question of direction is not decided by its counts. Version 2.1, reissued in place on 27 November 2026, widens the source from one book to a set of extant texts. It reads the letters and Josephus against Matthew by the same method, finds the letters' material concentrated in Matthew's discourses and Josephus's in its narrative, and sets out the account of Jesus son of Ananias in the *Jewish War* as twelve stations that fall in Matthew's order. It reads the Gospel of Thomas against Revelation and reports that Thomas and Matthew draw on the same verses of that book more often than their shared preference for its regions would give. The paper distinguishes a *derivation* (relations with stated moves, 28.6 per cent of Matthew's verses) from a *source map* (named pairs sharing words, 61.8 to 64.9 per cent), declines to suppose any hypothetical source for what remains, and classes every verse as recovered, composed or unexplained. It states that the order of composition is not shown by its counts.

defines_concepts.definition: In EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01, the transform that takes a relation in Revelation to a relation in Matthew: the source held whole with the relation as its unit, three parameters, seven moves on who bears a relation, five forms and five checks, twenty-one rules in all, stated at version 0.4.

In EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01, the paper's evidence: 86 rows, each a relation in Revelation and a relation in Matthew with their bearers, the lemmas both places hold as checked in a tagged text, the move that joins them and the standing of the row.

In EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01, the third mode of inheritance: a member that the source dropped when it compressed its own antecedent (scripture, Philo) is present again in the target, at the place the target opens.

In EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01, the rule that at each place of the source the layers it was made from stand open, so that a compressed member may be restored; Philo is admitted only through a place Revelation holds and a row has located.

In EA-REVFIRST-MATTHEW-01, the account of how a writer uses a known book: any place drawn on at any point of the new work, several at once and the same place twice, with the relation and not the sequence as the unit.
